newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Caution hangs over many Asian stock markets.
newsitem.headline: Caution hangs over many Asian stock markets.

text.p: Consolidation and caution seem likely to be the watchwords in most Asian stock markets in coming days, especially as many centres have a holiday-shortened trading period, analysts said.
In Japan, investors see a host of warning bells, while in Hong Kong, punters are digesting the government's moves to cool the key property sector.
Brighter prospects are seen in Bombay, as the new financial year approaches on April 1, and in Manila as traders position themselves for a series of first quarter earnings.
TOKYO - The Tokyo stock market is expected to be in cautious mood in the coming week as investors navigate their way through potential land mines, brokers said.

Brokers said they expect the 225-share Nikkei average to end the 1996/97 business year on March 31 within the 18,000 to 18,500 range, much in line with expectations. In the previous year, the benchmark finished at 21,406.85.

"There are worries about a decrease in unrealised profits of stocks held by firms, but as long as the index is within the range, a meltdown of the financial system, which is what the market is really paranoid of, can be avoided," a fund manager at a foreign investment advisory firm said.
On Friday, the Nikkei average finished down 20.70 points or 0.11 percent at 18,189.72. The index was down nearly 450 points from the previous Friday.
HONG KONG - Hong Kong stocks look set for further consolidation in the week ahead after a government move to curb real estate prices left investors fearing further clamps on the property market.
"This policy is making people concerned about the future policy of the government -- whether they will make another move," said Sunny Chan, senior research manager at Seapower Securities.
The Hang Seng Index rose 45.02 points, or 0.36 percent, in the past week but ended the abbreviated week on a shaky note on Thursday, tumbling 242.07 points or 1.89 percent to 12,534.32.
The market will close on Monday for the Easter Monday holiday.
BANGKOK - The Thai stock market is expected to fall slightly on thin turnover in the coming week due to a lack of incentives to persuade investors to enter the market, brokers said.

"Foreign investors are not expected to be active as most of them still take a holiday on Monday for Easter. Local investors will do the same as they await for inflation figures to be released by the commerce ministry early next week," said Kasem Prunratanamala of James Capel Asia.
The Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET) index gained about one percent in the past week to 709.09 points on Friday from a week earlier.
BOMBAY - Indian shares are expected to recover in the coming week with fresh demand picking up at the start of new fiscal year beginning April 1, brokers said.
"Software and telecommunication stocks could lead an upswing because foreign funds are bullish in these sectors," Yogendra Shah, director at YSN Shares Pvt Ltd said.
The 30-share Bombay Stock Exchange ended 66.67 points, or 1.79 percent, lower at 3,663.53 in the week to Friday.
DHAKA - Market analysts said the market would remain jittery over allegations of price manipulations by some brokers and companies.
The DSE benchmark index lost 116.27 points at 1,157.58 in the week to Thursday.
JAKARTA - Jakarta share prices are expected to be mixed in the coming week, with the likely focus on second-liners and newly-listed companies.

Brokers said trading would be active and the index was expected to be boosted by improved sentiment on blue chips such Telkom following a government confirmation that it had no intention of abolishing Telkom's monopoly ahead of schedule.

On Friday, the Jakarta Composite Index closed 2.84 points, or 0.43 percent, higher at 662.24 points, against the previous Friday's close of 656.11. The index was down about 0.9 percent, or 6.13 points on the week.
KARACHI - Pakistani stocks are likely to remain depressed owing to selling pressure in an overbought market, dealers at Karachi Stock Exchange (KCA) said.
Outstanding long trading positions are likely to increase selling pressure, dealer Zubair Ellahi said. "Stock prices are likely to remain depressed in the next few trading sessions."
On Friday, the index closed 17.55 points lower at 1,598.94 amid 49 losers and 13 gainers compared to a rise of 10.47 points, or 0.66 percent, to 1,592.75 on March 21.
KUALA LUMPUR - Analysts said the market would continue to trade cautiously in the coming week, as it digests the impact of Bank Negara's 1996 annual report.

"The market will be very cautious after the announcement of limits on share financing in Bank Negara's report. The restrictions could extend to unit trusts," said Victor Wan, senior analyst at South Johor Securities in Kuala Lumpur.
"These are all measures to cool the market down," he added.

For the week ended Friday March 28, the benchmark Composite Index of 100 large-capitalised stocks closed 4.70 points higher to 1,217.64 from 1,212.94 on March 14. From Thursday, the index fell 5.67 points.

MANILA - The Philippine equities market is expected to show further strength in the coming week as investors trek back to the market, positioning themselves ahead of the release of a slew of first quarter earnings and stockholders' meetings, traders said.

Jose Ricardo Garcia, executive vice-president at Diversified Securities Inc, said liquidity siphoned off by the Equitable Bank initial public offering will return with the listing of the bank's offering on April 3.
On Wednesday, the last day of trading before the Lenten season, the main index settled at 3,223.14 points, 21.49 points higher from the previous Friday's close of 3,201.65.
SEOUL - The Seoul stock market is expected to rise further in the coming week, but some analysts warned that potentially negative factors were lingering in the market.
"Increasing customer deposits and a small volume of new issues are the main factors to boost sentiment next week," said Park Byung-moon, research manager at LG Securities.
Potentially negative factors included a renewed probe into a loans-for-kickbacks scandal over failed Hanbo Steel Co.
The composite index closed at 652.87 on Friday, up four percent or 25.24 points from the previous Friday's 627.63.
SINGAPORE - Consolidation was seen in the Singapore stock market with buying sentiment likely to be depressed in the week ahead.
"We're still not out of the reporting season. The results so far have been uncertain and show that we're still in a low point for the economy," said a dealer with a local firm.
"I think we'll be taking our lead from the U.S. next week. If Wall Street doesn't do much, neither will we," he added.
The barometer Straits Times Industrials Index ended a trading week shortened by the Good Friday holiday at 2,098.92 on Thursday, up 30.44 on the previous week's close.
SYDNEY - Australian shares are seen taking their direction from the U.S. market after a four-day Easter break, with continued interest in banking stocks.
The All Ordinaries index gained 35.9 points, or 1.5 percent, to close on Thursday at 2,422.3, ending on a firm note as brokers squared their books ahead of the holiday.
Traders said attention would centre on bank stocks, which rose 2.2 percent in the past week, ahead of the expected release of the Wallis report into the financial system.
The report is widely expected to trigger big bank mergers if it recommends further bank deregulation and the government accepts its recommendations.
TAIPEI - Taiwan share prices are seen consolidating in the coming week due to a lack of strong market-moving factors.
The benchmark stock index has rebounded since Wednesday following a freefall on Monday and Tuesday over the outbreak of hog foot-and-mouth disease and an export ban on pork.
"The market sentiment should remain next week, but profit-taking is inevitable, thus resulting in a consolidation phase," Amy Huang of Nomura Securities said.
A trading range of 7,900-8,300 is seen for the coming week, brokers said.

WELLINGTON - New Zealand shares face the prospect of another quieter, holiday-shortened week. With the Telecom buyback dropping out in the coming week, turnover could also be expected to drop off, brokers said.

Paul Nicolson at SBC Warburg said trading would nevertheless be interesting with the buyback temporarily out of the equation. The average investor could suggest Telecom's price might slide without the buyback in place.
"But the other side of the coin would be that sellers might not be nearly as active," he said.
The NZSE-40 Capital Index ended the past week at 2,236.74, up 15.87 points from Thursday's close and a 6.95 point improvement on the previous Friday's 2,229.79 close.
